The proposition that textual meaning escapes the full determination of authorial intention finds its first rigorous support in the classic formulation of the intentional fallacy by Wimsatt and Beardsley. Their argument does not merely caution against biographical speculation; it fundamentally reorients our understanding of the literary work as a public, linguistic artifact. Once a poem or novel is committed to language, it is released into a system of signification that operates according to conventions, syntactic rules, and semantic fields that predate and will outlast any single author. The author may have chosen the words, but the meaning of those words is not a private possession; it is a product of shared usage, grammatical constraints, and the tacit interpretive protocols that govern how a given language community reads, infers, and connects. Irony, metaphor, and allusion, for instance, derive their effect not from the author’s inner state but from the reader’s recognition of deviation from or compliance with established linguistic norms. The author cannot legislate these norms, nor can they override the public character of language at will; their intention, however vivid to them, is merely one input into a much larger and more stable machinery of meaning that belongs to the collective, not the individual.

This inherent instability is deepened by the irreducible hermeneutic gap between conscious intent and semantic encoding, a gap that ensures authorial intention always underdetermines the full richness of textual meaning. Even when we grant that an author had a clear purpose, the linguistic tokens they deploy are finite and general, yet the interpretive elaborations those tokens invite are indefinite and context-sensitive. A simple declarative sentence can be read as assertion, hypothesis, irony, or quotation depending on tonal and intertextual cues that are not themselves part of the sentence’s literal proposition; similarly, a narrative event can be construed as tragic, comic, or allegorical without violating any grammatical or lexical fact about the text. The author’s conscious mind selects among possibilities, but it does not exhaust them, nor does it eliminate the logical compatibility of the same words with multiple divergent readings. This underdetermination is not a failure of craft but a structural feature of language itself, which operates through schemata and prototypes that invite filling-in by the reader. The author may have intended a specific emotional response or moral judgment, yet the text’s semantic potential includes pathways that the author never envisaged, precisely because meaning is not a one-to-one ciphering of mental content into words but a generative process wherein each utterance opens onto a horizon of possible interpretations constrained only by the linguistic system, not by the originating psyche.

The final and most radical claim, advanced by Barthes in his proclamation of the ‘death of the author,’ does not demand that we eliminate the author from literary history, but rather that we dethrone them from the position of interpretive sovereign. Read as a thesis about authority rather than ontology, Barthes’s insight is that textual meaning is not a buried treasure to be excavated from the author’s biography or psychology, but an event that unfolds in the act of reading. The reader brings to the text a repertoire of competences—cultural knowledge, literary memory, affective predispositions, and even unconscious associations—that are neither uniform across individuals nor stable over time. A text read in the seventeenth century yields different resonances than the same text read today, not because the words have changed, but because the interpretive frames, historical analogies, and ethical preoccupations of the reader have shifted. The author, confined to their own moment and limited by their own self-understanding, cannot possibly anticipate these future activations; they cannot intend what has not yet become thinkable. Consequently, the meaning that truly matters is the meaning that emerges in the dynamic encounter between text and reader, an encounter that is perpetually renewed and perpetually variable. This does not render interpretation arbitrary, for the text still constrains, but it does mean that the ultimate arbiter of significance is the living act of comprehension, not a dead or absent intention. The author’s original plan becomes one historical artifact among many, interesting but not dispositive, while the text’s vitality lies precisely in its capacity to signify beyond, and sometimes against, what its maker once hoped to say.
